modules.title: Automate deployment of resources by using Azure Resource Manager (ARM) templates or Bicep files

reveal.text: Azure Resource Manager (ARM) templates and Bicep files are declarative infrastructure-as-code formats for describing the Azure resources you want. ARM templates use JSON; Bicep is a concise Azure-specific language that compiles to ARM templates.
Infrastructure as code makes deployments repeatable and reviewable instead of relying on manual portal clicks.

cells.purpose: Change deployment values without rewriting resource logic
Describe resources and their configurable properties

reveal.text: When the task says “repeatable deployment,” “modify a template,” or “Bicep/ARM,” think declarative desired state rather than an imperative click sequence.

nodes.title: Deploy, export, and decompile infrastructure as code

reveal.text: A deployment submits an ARM template or Bicep file to a scope such as a resource group. Export can generate an ARM template from existing resources, while Bicep decompile converts ARM JSON to Bicep as a starting point.
These tools help move between an existing environment and reusable source-controlled infrastructure code, but generated output still needs review.

items: Inspect the existing resource or source template
Export ARM JSON when starting from deployed resources
Decompile ARM JSON to Bicep when Bicep is desired
Review parameters, names, dependencies, and generated code
Deploy to the intended scope and validate the result

reveal.text: Export/decompile is not guaranteed to produce perfect production-ready source. Review generated code before using it as the authoritative configuration.

nodes.title: Create a virtual machine: image, size, disks, and network

reveal.text: An Azure virtual machine (VM) is an on-demand virtual server. Creating one means choosing a workload image, compute size, storage, authentication, and network placement.
These choices determine what the VM runs, how much compute it has, where persistent data lives, and how it communicates.

cells.purpose: Operating system or prebuilt workload starting point
vCPU, memory, supported features, and throughput limits

reveal.text: A resize changes the VM SKU/capacity. Adding a managed data disk changes storage capacity. Network placement solves connectivity; these settings are not interchangeable.

source_refs.title: Study guide for Exam AZ-104: Microsoft Azure Administrator

nodes.title: Encryption at host for Azure VMs

reveal.text: Encryption at host performs encryption on the VM host for supported virtual machines, covering temporary disks and disk caches and ensuring data sent from the host to the Storage service is encrypted.
It expands the encryption boundary beyond standard server-side encryption of managed disks by protecting additional data handled on the compute host.

items: Enable it only on supported VM sizes/configurations.
Use it when the requirement explicitly includes temporary disks or disk caches.
Do not confuse encryption with access authorization; encryption does not grant VM permissions.

reveal.text: “Encrypt cache or temporary disk at the host” is a strong clue for encryption at host. Standard storage encryption alone is a different layer.

Server-side encryption of Azure managed disks

reveal.text: Azure resources can sometimes be moved between resource groups or subscriptions without changing region, but each resource type and dependency has move constraints. Moving a workload to another Azure region is a different migration operation.
Move planning prevents a partial migration in which a VM is separated from required dependent resources or an unsupported move is attempted.

columns.title: Resource group / subscription move
items: Usually keeps the resource in its current region
Validate dependencies and supported resource types
Move related resources together when required

columns.title: Cross-region move
items: Changes geographic region
Requires a regional migration approach such as Azure Resource Mover or workload-specific replication/migration
Plan downtime, dependencies, and destination capacity

reveal.text: A resource-group move does not mean a region change. If the destination is another region, choose a regional migration mechanism.

reveal.text: Availability zones are physically separate datacenter locations within a supported Azure region. Availability sets spread VMs across fault and update domains to reduce correlated hardware/maintenance impact within a datacenter-oriented deployment model.
Both improve availability, but zones provide stronger physical datacenter isolation when the region and workload support them.

columns.title: Availability zone
items: Separate datacenter-level location within a region
Use zonal or zone-redundant architecture when supported
Protect against a zone-level failure

columns.title: Availability set
items: Groups VMs across fault and update domains
Useful for multiple VMs that are not deployed across zones
Reduces shared hardware/maintenance failure risk

reveal.text: If the requirement explicitly says “datacenter failure” or “separate facilities in one region,” availability zones are the stronger clue.

reveal.text: Azure Virtual Machine Scale Sets create and manage a group of virtual machines from a common configuration. The group can add or remove instances as demand changes and can integrate with load balancing.
VMSS is useful when many similar VM instances should behave like one scalable compute tier.

items: Define a scale-set model
Create multiple similar VM instances
Distribute client traffic through a supported load-balancing design
Apply scaling rules or capacity changes
Replace or update instances while preserving the group model

reveal.text: “Many identical VMs,” “autoscale VM instances,” or “scale a VM-based application tier” points to VMSS rather than one standalone VM.

modules.title: Provision and manage containers in the Azure portal

reveal.text: Azure Container Registry is a managed private registry for storing and managing container images and OCI-compatible artifacts.
A registry separates the image-distribution problem from the runtime that executes the containers.

columns.title: Azure Container Registry
items: Stores images/artifacts
Controls registry access and image distribution
Does not by itself run an application

columns.title: Container runtime service
items: Pulls an image and runs containers
Provides CPU/memory/networking at runtime
Examples include ACI and Container Apps

reveal.text: If the requirement is “private image repository,” choose ACR. If the requirement is “run this image,” you need a runtime service too.

source_refs.title: Study guide for Exam AZ-104: Microsoft Azure Administrator
Azure Container Registry documentation

reveal.text: Azure Container Instances runs container groups directly in Azure without requiring you to manage virtual machines or a Kubernetes cluster. You choose resources such as CPU and memory for the container group.
ACI is useful for simple or bursty container workloads where a full application platform or orchestrator would add unnecessary complexity.

items: Deploy an image from a registry.
Specify CPU, memory, networking, environment variables, and other runtime settings.
Create additional container groups or automate deployments when more instances are needed.

reveal.text: “Run a container quickly without managing servers or an orchestrator” is an ACI clue. Do not assume ACI has the same revision/autoscaling model as Container Apps.

source_refs.title: Study guide for Exam AZ-104: Microsoft Azure Administrator
Azure Container Instances documentation

reveal.text: Azure Container Apps is a managed serverless container application platform. It supports application revisions, ingress, environment boundaries, and scaling rules driven by HTTP traffic or supported event sources.
It provides more application-platform behavior than ACI while hiding most cluster infrastructure from the administrator.

cells.scaling: Size a container group; create/manage additional groups as needed
Configure min/max replicas and HTTP/event-driven rules

reveal.text: Revisions, ingress, and event/HTTP-driven replica scaling are strong Container Apps clues.

modules.title: Create and configure Azure App Service

nodes.title: App Service plans and web apps

reveal.text: Azure App Service hosts web applications and APIs on managed platform compute. An App Service plan defines the region and compute resources used by apps in that plan.
Separating the app from its hosting plan helps you reason about where compute cost, capacity, and scaling are controlled.

columns.title: Web app
items: Application configuration and deployed code
App settings, custom domains, TLS, deployment slots

columns.title: App Service plan
items: Underlying managed compute for one or more apps
Pricing tier, instance size/count, supported capabilities

reveal.text: If a question asks to change the compute tier or instance capacity, look at the App Service plan rather than only the app resource.

source_refs.title: Study guide for Exam AZ-104: Microsoft Azure Administrator

nodes.title: Scale up versus scale out in App Service

reveal.text: Scaling up changes the App Service plan to a different pricing tier or larger compute size. Scaling out changes how many worker instances serve the application.
The distinction matters because one solves per-instance capacity/capability limits while the other adds parallel instances.

columns.title: Scale up
items: Bigger or different tier/size
More capability per worker
May unlock plan features

columns.title: Scale out
items: More worker instances
Distribute workload across instances
Can use manual or autoscale behavior depending on plan/support

reveal.text: “Need more memory per instance” suggests scale up. “Need more parallel instances during traffic spikes” suggests scale out.

nodes.title: Custom domains, DNS, certificates, and TLS

reveal.text: An App Service custom domain maps a DNS name you own to the application. HTTPS then uses an appropriate certificate binding and TLS configuration for that hostname.
DNS proves where clients should connect; the certificate protects and authenticates the HTTPS connection. They solve different parts of the request path.

items: Add/verify the custom domain mapping
Create the required DNS record at the authoritative DNS provider
Provision or upload a suitable certificate
Bind the certificate to the hostname for TLS
Test HTTPS and renewal/expiration behavior

reveal.text: A CNAME/A record alone does not provide HTTPS. A certificate alone does not make the public DNS name resolve to the app.

nodes.title: Backups, networking, and deployment slots in App Service

reveal.text: App Service provides operational features for protecting app data/configuration, controlling network paths, and staging deployments. Backups preserve supported app content/configuration, networking features control inbound/outbound connectivity, and deployment slots create separate live environments that can be swapped.
These features reduce release risk and help connect a managed web app to private or controlled resources without turning it into a VM.

cells.job: Control inbound access and outbound connectivity to networks/resources
cells.clue: Reach private backend or restrict app access

cells.job: Stage and validate another app version before swap

reveal.text: If the requirement is safer releases, deployment slots are the clue. If the requirement is private backend connectivity, use App Service networking features.
